name: Program Evaluation
title: Program Evaluation
answer: Program evaluation is the practice of checking whether a program or tool actually works by comparing students who used it with similar students who did not. It matters because without that comparison a district cannot tell whether gains came from the program or from something else, and because honest findings, including disappointing ones, free money and time for better options. It also keeps expectations realistic and asks vendors with dramatic claims for evidence.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: Districts spend money on programs and tools, so they need to know what works. The pilot method described in Chapter 4 applies to every program. The strongest evaluations compare students who used a program with similar students who did not. Without a comparison, a district cannot tell whether gains came from the program or from something else. This idea solves the problem of spending without evidence and sets realistic expectations, since most education programs that work produce effects in a similar range.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, program evaluation starts by applying the pilot method to any program under consideration. Teams compare students who used the program with similar students who did not, so they can see whether the program made a difference. For students receiving extra help, intervention results tracking shows whether they are catching up. Multi tiered systems of support platforms can track each student's progress through interventions, and AI can help teams see which interventions are working for which students. The team then decides whether to continue, change, or end an intervention, and the text's only grade band reference is K through 12 math, where tutoring and adaptive systems showed larger effects.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book's evidence for this idea is a meta analysis of AI in K through 12 math. It found a small positive effect of about 0.34 standard deviations, larger for tutoring and adaptive systems (Yi et al., 2024). The text adds that most education programs that work produce effects in a similar range. It also says a vendor promising dramatic gains should be asked for evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that a district cannot attribute gains without a comparison group. Expectations should be realistic, and a vendor promising dramatic gains should be asked for evidence. The decision to continue, change, or end an intervention stays with the team, not with the AI. Evaluation findings should be shared honestly, including disappointing ones, because a program that did not work is valuable information that frees money and time for something better. Districts that report only successes lose credibility, and boards and families deserve the full picture.
